premise: A period drama set at MIT in 1966, the year Joseph Weizenbaum built ELIZA.
title: ELIZA · 1966
overview: The research reveals MIT in 1966 as an environment of massive mainframe hardware, military funding, and early time-sharing networks. Joseph Weizenbaum built the ELIZA program inside Project MAC to demonstrate the superficial nature of natural language processing. Users immediately attributed genuine empathy to the program and formed deep emotional bonds with the terminal. The film follows Weizenbaum as he discovers his shipped software functions as a psychological trap. He turns against his own creation and rejects the praise of his colleagues.

boxes.name: COMPUTING HARDWARE INTERFACES
boxes.description: Archival floor plans, maintenance logs, and photographs document the physical footprint, console lamps, tape drives, and acoustic output of the IBM 7094 and compatible time-sharing systems at Project MAC in 1966.
boxes.rationale: The technical crew needs precise mechanical specifications to fabricate working teleprinter terminals and simulate computer operations on set.
boxes.summary: The IBM 7094 mainframe occupied an entire machine room at Project MAC. The installation required arrays of magnetic tape units, raised flooring for cabling, and a master console covered in indicator lamps. Operators relied on the Compatible Time-Sharing System to run programs from remote terminals. The machine generated a constant acoustic hum from internal cooling systems. The console lights shifted patterns as the computer processed discrete batch jobs and time-sharing cycles.

boxes.name: PROJECT MAC ARCHITECTURE
boxes.description: Blueprints, office assignments, and interior photographs record the institutional aesthetic of Tech Square and Building 26 during the mid-nineteen-sixties.
boxes.rationale: The production designer must replicate the specific cinderblock walls, linoleum flooring, and fluorescent lighting arrangements that defined Weizenbaum's actual work environment.
boxes.summary: Project MAC occupied multiple floors inside the Technology Square complex near the MIT campus. The ninth floor housed the artificial intelligence laboratory with concrete floors, fluorescent ceiling strips, and modular office dividers. Architecture of the era favored bare painted walls, heavy metal desks, and institutional acoustic tiles. Building 26 and Tech Square served as functional engineering workspaces. Researchers worked behind standard institutional doors along central corridors.

boxes.name: ACADEMIC LAB CODES
boxes.description: Oral histories, student yearbooks, and faculty memoirs record the daily attire of senior computer scientists, graduate research assistants, and clerical staff at mid-decade MIT.
boxes.rationale: Costume designers need accurate references to dress the cast according to their exact status within the technical hierarchy.
boxes.summary: Faculty members dressed in dark wool suits, narrow ties, and short-sleeved collared shirts. Graduate research assistants wore casual cotton button-downs, slacks, and occasional work boots. Clerical workers wore modest dresses or skirts consistent with mid-decade office dress codes. Student yearbooks show clean-cut appearances alongside a growing number of unkempt hairstyles. Staff members wore laminated identification badges pinned to shirt pockets.

boxes.name: DEPARTMENTAL FUNDING APPARATUS
boxes.description: Declassified DARPA grant paperwork and administrative correspondence establish the military financial networks that sustained MIT computer research during the Vietnam War.
boxes.rationale: The screenwriters need documented institutional relationships to ground the ethical conflicts surrounding military-sponsored computing.
boxes.summary: The Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency funded Project MAC through the Information Processing Techniques Office. Research proposals and technical reports flowed directly between Cambridge and the Department of Defense. Administrative files record regular contract renewals to develop advanced time-sharing systems. The computing laboratory operated on federal money during the height of the Vietnam War. Faculty members drafted periodic progress reports to justify their military grants.

boxes.name: CAMBRIDGE SOUND ENVIRONMENT
boxes.description: Field recordings, industrial archives, and transit documentation define the balance of acoustic noise from cooling blowers, teletype ribbons, street traffic, and urban construction in 1966.
boxes.rationale: The sound team must build a historically accurate auditory layer that distinguishes machine rooms from exterior Cambridge neighborhoods.
boxes.summary: Mainframe cooling blowers generated persistent background drone levels between 35 and 44 decibels inside the labs. Model 33 teletypewriters produced continuous mechanical clatter, paper tearing sounds, and ribbon impacts. External streets in Kendall Square carried diesel bus exhaust, braking sounds, and standard vehicular traffic. Industrial machinery and urban construction added low-frequency rumbles across Cambridge. The interior workspace remained filled with the rhythmic clicking of relays and keypunches.

boxes.name: CAMPUS RADICAL POLITICS
boxes.description: Underground campus newspapers, rally flyers, and local police surveillance logs detail the emergence of antiwar protests and New Left organizing at MIT and Harvard in 1966.
boxes.rationale: The script and background casting teams require specific political banners, chants, and participant profiles to stage historical demonstrations outside the laboratories.
boxes.summary: Underground student newspapers circulated across Cambridge with antiwar declarations and protest dates. Student activists organized rallies in Boston Common and picketed university buildings tied to military research. Local and state police maintained surveillance files on campus peace movement organizers. Demonstrators confronted government officials visiting Harvard and MIT throughout 1966. Handbills and bedsheet banners documented growing student resistance to defense-sponsored lab work.

boxes.name: TECH LINGUISTIC JARGON
boxes.description: Glossaries from the Tech Model Railroad Club and contemporary software manuals capture the emerging hacker lexicon, LISP programming terms, and psychiatric vocabulary of the era.
boxes.rationale: The screenwriters and actors need authentic laboratory speech patterns to deliver persuasive technical dialogue.
boxes.summary: The Tech Model Railroad Club established early computer slang including the word hacker. Programmers communicated using specific terms derived from the LISP language and CTSS operating system. Technical manuals defined operational commands alongside informal lab jargon. Staff adapted psychiatric phrasing into program labels and script commands. The resulting technical dialect mixed engineering shorthand with conversational English.

boxes.name: CLERICAL LABOR ROUTINES
boxes.description: Personnel files, interview transcripts, and time sheets document the daily duties, salaries, and social backgrounds of the women who operated punch cards and transcribed lab notes.
boxes.rationale: Writers and set dressers must accurately represent the gendered administrative labor that enabled early software experimentation.
boxes.summary: Female keypunch operators prepared stacks of eighty-column punched cards for daily mainframe input. Clerical workers transcribed handwritten faculty drafts, debugged program listings, and sorted printouts. Time sheets recorded long operational shifts spent at mechanical card punch machines. These women managed daily data entry routines that kept the larger computing projects functional. Staff members maintained strict logging procedures for every submitted card deck.

boxes.name: COMMUTER TRANSIT ARTERIES
boxes.description: Municipal transportation records and street photography map the MBTA Red Line operations, bus lines, and vehicular traffic between Boston and Kendall Square in 1966.
boxes.rationale: The location manager needs period-accurate urban streets and transit hubs to stage Weizenbaum's daily commute.
boxes.summary: The MBTA Red Line connected central Boston to Kendall Station via subterranean trains. Commuters walked from subway portals into the industrial grid of Main Street. Municipal buses and private automobiles shared surface traffic corridors across the Charles River. Transit schedules dictated the arrival and departure times of non-resident staff. Kendall Square functioned as an active transit nexus between campus facilities and local residential districts.

boxes.name: DOMESTIC FACULTY LIFE
boxes.description: Real estate listings, retail catalogs, and domestic photographs establish the home furnishings, grocery brands, and leisure activities common to middle-class academic families in contemporary Middlesex County.
boxes.rationale: The art and props departments must furnish the protagonist's private residence to reflect his economic standing outside the institute.
boxes.summary: Faculty residences in Middlesex County featured single-family suburban layouts with wood siding. Interiors contained mid-century furniture, Heywood-Wakefield wood chairs, and wool rugs. Academic households stored mass-market consumer packaged goods and local groceries in utilitarian kitchens. Domestic life centered around dinner tables, home study desks, and standard television sets. Faculty members commuted between these domestic neighborhoods and their Cambridge offices.

boxes.name: PSYCHIATRIC THERAPY DISCOURSE
boxes.description: Clinical intake forms, Carl Rogers transcripts, and contemporary psychiatric journals document the Rogerian non-directive counseling techniques, therapeutic phrasing, and ethical debates simulated by Weizenbaum's DOCTOR script.
boxes.rationale: This discourse directly intersects with the computational linguistic jargon, clerical staff interactions with the ELIZA console, and faculty ideological debates surrounding the psychological ethics of military-funded computing.
boxes.summary: The DOCTOR script inside ELIZA simulated Carl Rogers' non-directive psychotherapy techniques. The program parsed patient text to identify keywords and reflected them back as open-ended questions. Rogerian therapy relied on reflective listening without offering direct advice or diagnostic labels. Users treated the program as an authentic therapist and confided personal secrets to the screen. The resulting transcripts simulated a clinical intake session using minimal linguistic rules.

## Introduction

This article describes MIT's Project MAC, the organization that led the initial creation of Multics.
This is not a comprehensive history of Project MAC:
my goal is to provide context and motivation for Multics history, and to provide accurate statements and references for deeper investigation. (The author was a part-time undergraduate programmer and then a research staff member at Project MAC during its first seven years.)

## Background

### MIT environment

Thu, 05/14/1964 - 12:00

One of the first major efforts supported by ARPA's Information Processing Techniques Office (IPTO) was the Project on Mathematics and Computation (Project MAC), the world’s first large-scale experiment in personal computing, at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT). Orchestrated within the general context of broad-based command and control research suggested by the Office of the Secretary of Defense, and based on the vision of the founding IPTO Director, J.C.R. Licklider, Project MAC was oriented toward achieving a new level of human-computer interaction. A major thrust of Project MAC was to develop general purpose time-sharing capabilities, which later influenced the design of computer systems for commercial and defense uses. Within years of its start, Project MAC would evolve into the world’s first online community, complete with online bulletin boards, email, virtual friendships, an open-source software exchange—and hackers.

Anti-war student activists clashed with politicians and University administrators as the nation grappled with one of the most controversial wars in the country’s history.

By Laszlo B. Herwitz

* * *

As a freshman, Richard E. Hyland ’69 was not particularly attuned to Cold War politics. While students at the College protested the United States’s campaign in Vietnam, Hyland did not identify with the anti-war movement.

One day, though, Hyland found a small leaflet slipped under the door of his freshman suite.

“The leaflet said ‘If you’re for the war in Vietnam, why aren’t you fighting it, and if you’re against the war in Vietnam, why aren’t you in the streets fighting against it with us?’” Hyland said.

Inspired by the leaflet, Hyland rushed to the periodical reading room in Lamont and began to study Vietnam. Soon, Hyland knew he wanted to join the anti-war movement at Harvard.

In the late 1960s, students, professors, and administrators were sharply divided over the war. Anti-war student activists clashed with politicians and University administrators as the nation grappled with one of the most brutal—and controversial—wars in the country’s history.

Hackers  We at TMRC use the term "hacker" only in its original meaning, someone who
applies ingenuity to create a clever result, called a "hack". The essence
of a "hack" is that it is done quickly, and is usually inelegant. It
accomplishes the desired goal without changing the design of the system it
is embedded in. Despite often being at odds with the design of the larger
system, a hack is generally quite clever and effective.

 This original benevolent meaning stands in stark contrast to the later and
more commonly used meaning of a "hacker", typically as a person
who breaks into computer networks in order to steal or vandalize. Here at
TMRC, where the words "hack" and "hacker" originated and have been used
proudly since the late 1950s, we resent the misapplication of the
word to mean the committing of illegal acts. People who do those things are
better described by expressions such as "thieves", "password crackers". or
"computer vandals". They are certainly not true hackers, as they do not
understand the hacker ethic.

 Also see the [definition of "hacker" in the on-line version of the New Hacker's Dictionary](http://catb.org/~esr/jargon/html/H/hacker.html) .

Hollerith’s 1890 census device proved the feasibility of punched cards for big projects. And his Tabulating Machine Company helped make cards the primary data storage system for 80 years. But Hollerith didn’t invent the idea. In the early 1800s, mechanized looms stored textile patterns using punched cards. Charles Babbage’s un-built Analytical Engine featured a card reader. Middlesex is an inland county in the south of England. Middlesex has long been dominated by its two great cities: London and Westminster. By the early 20th-century the metropolitan area around these had spread west to Chiswick; north to Highgate; and across the Lea into Essex and the Thames into Surrey. Beyond this, most of Middlesex remained rural, its farmland and villages interspersed between its main towns: Willesden, Acton, Ealing, Brentford, Hounslow, Isleworth, Twickenham, Teddington, Staines, Uxbridge, Harrow on the Hill, Edgware, Tottenham and Edmonton. The 20th century saw much of Middlesex become part of the metropolitan conurbation. Hackers  We at TMRC use the term "hacker" only in its original meaning, someone who
applies ingenuity to create a clever result, called a "hack". The essence
of a "hack" is that it is done quickly, and is usually inelegant. It
accomplishes the desired goal without changing the design of the system it
is embedded in. Despite often being at odds with the design of the larger
system, a hack is generally quite clever and effective.

 This original benevolent meaning stands in stark contrast to the later and
more commonly used meaning of a "hacker", typically as a person
who breaks into computer networks in order to steal or vandalize. Here at
TMRC, where the words "hack" and "hacker" originated and have been used
proudly since the late 1950s, we resent the misapplication of the
word to mean the committing of illegal acts. People who do those things are
better described by expressions such as "thieves", "password crackers". or
"computer vandals". They are certainly not true hackers, as they do not
understand the hacker ethic.

 Also see the [definition of "hacker" in the on-line version of the New Hacker's Dictionary](http://catb.org/~esr/jargon/html/H/hacker.html) .

Students in the Tech Model Railroad Club first used hack for clever improvements to train circuits, then applied it to creative computer work. # Joseph Weizenbaum

Computer Scientist Joseph Weizenbaum

**Profession:** Computer Scientist

**Nationality:** United States of America American

**Biography:** Joseph Weizenbaum was a German-American computer scientist who made significant contributions to the early development of artificial intelligence (AI) and computer programming. He is best known for creating ELIZA, an early natural language processing program that was able to engage in simple text-based conversations with users, giving the illusion of understanding and empathy.

Weizenbaum developed ELIZA in the mid-1960s, and the program's most famous iteration, known as "DOCTOR," simulated a Rogerian psychotherapist, responding to users' statements with questions and prompts. While ELIZA was not capable of true understanding or empathy, its ability to engage users in seemingly meaningful conversations raised important questions about the nature of human-computer interaction and the potential ethical implications of AI.

ELIZA is a pioneering natural language processing computer program created by Joseph Weizenbaum at MIT from 1964 to 1967. Designed as an experiment to explore human-machine communication, ELIZA operates using a clever pattern-matching and substitution methodology. This approach gives users the illusion of understanding, even though the program itself doesn't truly comprehend the meaning of the conversation. The most famous ELIZA script, DOCTOR , simulates a psychotherapist practicing Rogerian psychotherapy. It responds to user inputs with non-directional questions and reflections, often mirroring back the user's own statements. This script made ELIZA one of the earliest examples of a chatbot and a program capable of attempting the Turing Test.
